files.lesson.md: --- order: 11 unit: reals9 node: AC9M9N01 n2 uses: [AC9M9N01 n1] assumes: [AC9M8N01 n1, AC9M8N01 n2] connection: square-patch title: Exact or rounded? summary: "√2 is exact. 1.41 is only close. Keep the exact value, or the full calculator value, until the last step, and round at the end." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A calculator shows √50 as 7.0710678… and a builder cuts to 7.1 m. How wrong is that?" --- An irrational number never ends, so every decimal for it is a rounded version. The question is when rounding is fine. ## Predict: a rounded side ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to the area of a rounded square shows who thinks rounding the side to 7.1 m changes nothing, and who expects it to be a little bigger." check: type: predict q: "A square patch is meant to have an area of exactly 50 m², so its side is $\\sqrt{50}$ m. A builder rounds the side up to 7.1 m. What area does the patch actually have?" options: - "$50.41$ m²" - "$50$ m²" - "$49.0$ m²" - "$51.0$ m²" actual: "50.41 m². 7.1 × 7.1 = 50.41, a bit more than 50. √50 = 7.0710678…, so 7.1 is a little too big and squaring doubles the error's effect." ``` The vegetable patch should be exactly 50 m². What length is each side? ## Run: check on a calculator ```step stage: run insight: "Squaring a rounded side doesn't give back the exact area: the result is close but not exact." check: { type: number, q: "Use a calculator. What is $7.1 \\times 7.1$? Was your prediction right?", answer: 50.41, tolerance: 0.001, explain: "7.1² = 50.41, a little over 50." } ``` Press √50 on your calculator. The screen shows a rounded version of a number that never ends. ## Investigate: when rounding matters ```step stage: investigate insight: "Round at the end, not in the middle: each early rounding adds a small error that later steps can grow. Lee treats 2 × 1.4 as exact." tasks: - check: type: question q: "Which one keeps the exact value of the side?" options: ["$\\sqrt{50}$", "$7.07$", "$7.071$", "$7.1$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "7.07 is √50 rounded to 2 decimal places.", "7.071 is √50 rounded to 3 decimal places.", "7.1 is √50 rounded to 1 decimal place."] explain: "√50 is exact. Each decimal version is rounded." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#lee" text: "Lee works out the cable along 2 diagonals of a 1 m square. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: round-early explain: "Line 4: 2 × 1.4 = 2.8 is an approximation, because √2 was rounded. The exact length is 2√2 m, which is about 2.83 m." - check: type: number q: "Use exact values: what is $\\sqrt{50} \\times \\sqrt{50}$?" answer: 50 explain: "√50 × √50 = 50 exactly: a square root times itself gives the number back." ``` ### Exact first Here's the difference rounding early makes. ```worked \sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2} :: Exact: (√2)² = 2, so (√2)⁴ = 4. 1.4 \times 1.4 \times 1.4 \times 1.4 :: Rounded to 1 decimal place first. = 3.8416 :: Not 4. \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41421356 \text{, so } 1.41421356^4 \approx 4.0000 :: Keep more digits and it's closer. ``` Now try one on paper: use $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.4$ to work out $(\sqrt{2})^4$ by multiplying four 1.4s. Then type the value you get. ### Find the mistake Read Lee's working. Is 2.8 exact? ### Which is exact? ## Modify: change the rounding ```step stage: modify insight: "Changing how many places the side is rounded to: more places make the squared answer closer to 50. An exact form like 5√2 never needs rounding." tasks: - hint: ["Round √50 to 2 decimal places: 7.07.", "Then square it."] check: { type: number, q: "Round $\\sqrt{50}$ to 2 decimal places (7.07), then square it. What do you get?", answer: 49.98, tolerance: 0.01, explain: "7.07² = 49.9849, a little under 50." } smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "Just the first part: what's $7.07 \\times 7.07$ to the nearest whole number?", answer: 50, explain: "7.07 × 7.07 = 49.98…, which is about 50." } - hint: ["Round √50 to 3 decimal places: 7.071.", "Then square it."] check: { type: number, q: "Round $\\sqrt{50}$ to 3 decimal places (7.071), then square it. What do you get, to 1 decimal place?", answer: 50, tolerance: 0.05, explain: "7.071² = 49.999…, so 50.0 to 1 decimal place." } - hint: ["50 = 25 × 2.", "√25 = 5."] check: { type: question, q: "Edge case: which one is exactly equal to $\\sqrt{50}$?", options: ["$5\\sqrt{2}$", "$7\\sqrt{1}$", "$25\\sqrt{2}$", "$\\sqrt{25}$"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "7 × 1 = 7, but √50 is 7.07….", "5√2 squared is 50, but 25√2 squared is 1250.", "√25 = 5."], explain: "√50 = √(25 × 2) = √25 × √2 = 5√2. Both are exact." } ``` ### Two decimal places ### Three decimal places ### Another exact form ## Practise: decide ```step stage: practise insight: "Choosing between exact and rounded and rounding at the end; the review keeps the families straight." tasks: - check: type: number q: "The exact side of a square of area 20 m² is $\\sqrt{20}$. To 2 decimal places, what is it?" answer: 4.47 tolerance: 0.005 explain: "√20 = 4.4721…, so 4.47." - check: type: number q: "Edging goes round that square: 4 sides of $\\sqrt{20}$ m. Work it out with the full calculator value, then round to 1 decimal place." answer: 17.9 tolerance: 0.05 explain: "4 × 4.4721… = 17.888…, which is 17.9. Round at the end." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "Just the first step: what's $\\sqrt{20}$ to 2 decimal places?", answer: 4.47, tolerance: 0.005, explain: "√20 = 4.47 to 2 decimal places." } - check: type: question q: "A drawing says a part is $\\sqrt{2}$ m long. Which is best for the drawing?" options: ["Write √2", "Write 1.4", "Write 1.41", "Write 1.4142"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "1.4 is rounded: it loses information.", "1.41 is rounded.", "1.4142 is rounded: the drawing can stay exact."] explain: "On a drawing the exact value stays exact. The builder rounds when cutting." - check: type: question q: "Review: which is rational?" options: ["$\\sqrt{49}$", "$\\sqrt{50}$", "$\\sqrt{51}$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "50 isn't a perfect square.", "51 isn't a perfect square."] explain: "√49 = 7." ``` ### A square patch ### Edging ### A drawing ### Review Rational or irrational, from the last lesson. ## Make: back to the patch ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the patch: working with the exact value, then rounding once at the end, gives the edging length." tasks: - hint: ["Edging = 4 × the side.", "The side is √50. Use the calculator's full value, then round once."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A square patch has area 50 m². Work out the length of edging for all 4 sides, to 1 decimal place." steps: - ["$\\text{side} = \\sqrt{50}$", "exact value of the side"] - ["$4\\sqrt{50} = 28.2842\\ldots$", "use the full calculator value"] - ["$28.3$ m", "round once, at the end"] answer: "28.3" answerLabel: "Edging (m)" tolerance: 0.05 feedback: - ["28.4", "That's from rounding the side to 7.1 first. Round at the end."] - ["28", "Keep one decimal place: 28.3."] criteria: - "I used the exact value of the side." - "I rounded only once, at the end." - "My answer is close to 28.3." explain: "4 × 7.0710678… = 28.284…, so 28.3 m." - check: type: question q: "Why was 28.4 a worse answer than 28.3?" options: ["The side was rounded to 7.1 first", "28.4 isn't a number", "4 × 7.1 is wrong"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "It is a number: just not the best one.", "4 × 7.1 = 28.4: the arithmetic is right, but 7.1 was already rounded."] explain: "Rounding the side early adds an error that the multiplication then grows." ``` ### The edging Back to the patch. Work this out on paper first, then type your answer. ### Why 28.4? **Also used in** - **Building and design.** A drawing keeps √2, and the builder rounds to the nearest millimetre when cutting. - **Next lesson.** Where numbers sit on the line, and ranges of values like tolerances. ```teacher summary: Students tell exact values like √50 from rounded decimals, see rounding early change an answer, and decide when to keep an exact form or round (AC9M9N01, node 2). time: 35 timing: Predict and Run 6 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 9 min goals: - I can say whether a value is exact or rounded. - I can explain why rounding early causes errors. - I can round at the end of a calculation. struggle: Not rounding in the middle. Ask students to keep the calculator's full value, or write the exact form, until the last line. before: > Students need Number families. Calculators needed. The one idea: an exact value stays exact until the end; round once. The common mistake is rounding at the start and calling the result exact (Lee's working). The patch is made up: area 50 m². running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Those who chose 50 m² assumed 7.1 was the exact side." - "Run: ask students to press √50 on a calculator and read the digits aloud." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the edging in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for rounding at the last line only." - "Modify: before 7.07², ask if the answer will be more or less than 50." stuck: - see: A student rounds √50 to 7 and squares it. ask: What's 7 × 7? How far off is that from 50? fix: "49: round to more places, or keep the exact value." - see: A student writes 7.07 = √50. ask: Is 7.07 exactly the square root of 50? fix: "No: it's close. Use ≈." stretch: How many decimal places of √50 do you need so that squaring gives 50.00 to 2 places? support: "A card: 'exact' (√, π, fractions) and 'rounded' (decimals with ≈)." leads: | Continues AC9M9N01 node 2. Where it leads: tolerances and intervals (next), formulas with π and roots. exit: q: "Which is exact: √8 or 2.83?" a: √8. 2.83 is rounded. explain: > $\sqrt{50}$ is exact. 7.07 is rounded: close, but not equal. Keep the exact value or the calculator's full value through the calculation, and round once at the end. Rounding early adds a small error that later steps can grow. ```

# Lee's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: lee
A 1 m square has a diagonal of √2 m. Find the length of a cable that goes along 2 diagonals.
√2 is about 1.4.
2 diagonals: 2 × 1.4 = 2.8.
So the cable is exactly 2.8 m.
